question: What is the Tropic of Cancer?
shortAnswer: The Tropic of Cancer is the circle at {tilt}° north. On one day each year — the summer solstice, around {juneSolstice} — the Sun stands straight overhead on this line. North of it, the Sun is never straight overhead.

teasers./: The dashed gold line north of the equator on the map above — the Sun never stands overhead north of it.
teasers./earth/: The northern edge of the band where a flagpole can have no shadow.

ledeHtml: The Tropic of Cancer is the circle at {tilt}° north. This circle is where the Sun stands straight overhead — a flagpole there would cast no shadow — on the summer solstice, around {juneSolstice}. That is the longest day of the year in the north. The Sun is never straight overhead anywhere north of this line. The number {tilt}° is Earth’s tilt.
title: What Is the Tropic of Cancer?
description: The Tropic of Cancer is the circle at {tilt}° N. On the summer solstice, around {juneSolstice}, the Sun stands straight overhead there — and never north of it.
graphicCaption: Drawn at the summer solstice, around {juneSolstice}. Earth is leaning as far toward the Sun as it ever does. The yellow line from the Sun’s centre through Earth’s centre hits the Tropic of Cancer.
graphicAlt: Side view of the Sun and Earth at the summer solstice. Parallel sunlight from the left. A solid yellow line from the Sun’s centre through Earth’s centre hits the Tropic of Cancer. Dashed chords mark both tropics at plus and minus Earth’s tilt.

sections.heading: Why it sits at {tilt}° north
body: Earth does not sit straight up as it goes around the Sun. It leans about {tilt}°. That lean is Earth’s axial tilt, and it barely changes from one year to the next.

Because the axis keeps pointing the same way all year, the lean facing the Sun changes as Earth goes around. Around {juneSolstice} the north end leans as far into the light as it ever does. A ray from the centre of the Sun through the centre of Earth then hits this circle. That day is the summer solstice — the longest day of the year in the north. The picture above is that day.

sections.heading: Why {tilt}° — and why it is not a climate stripe
body: A climate map that colours a band “tropical” is a later idea. The tropic itself is a measurement: the maximum solar declination. If the tilt were 10°, the tropic would sit at 10° N. If the tilt were zero, both tropics would collapse onto the equator, and there would be no seasons.

The two circles are drawn on the map as dashed parallels at plus and minus the tilt. They do not move with the day. What moves is the yellow subsolar point, which runs a lap of longitude every 24 hours and a lap of latitude once a year, bouncing between those two dashed lines.

sections.heading: Why it is named Cancer
body: Two thousand years ago the Sun stood in the constellation Cancer at the June solstice. It no longer does. Earth’s axis slowly circles (precession), so the solstice Sun has drifted about a whole constellation since. The name stayed. The latitude is still exactly the tilt; only the star charts moved.

sections.heading: What the polar circles have to do with it
body: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles sit at 90° minus the same tilt — about 66.6° N and S. Inside them the Sun can fail to set in summer or fail to rise in winter. One number, four circles: two tropics and two polar circles. Change the tilt and all four move together.

question: What is the Tropic of Capricorn?
shortAnswer: The Tropic of Capricorn is the circle at {tilt}° south. On one day each year — the winter solstice, around {decSolstice} — the Sun stands straight overhead on this line. South of it, the Sun is never straight overhead. It is the southern twin of the Tropic of Cancer.
ledeHtml: The Tropic of Capricorn is the circle at {tilt}° south. This circle is where the Sun stands straight overhead — a flagpole there would cast no shadow — on the winter solstice, around {decSolstice}. That is the shortest day of the year in the north, and summer in the south. The Sun is never straight overhead anywhere south of this line. It is the southern twin of the Tropic of Cancer.
title: What Is the Tropic of Capricorn?
description: The Tropic of Capricorn is the circle at {tilt}° S. On the winter solstice, around {decSolstice}, the Sun stands straight overhead there — and never south of it.
graphicCaption: Drawn at the winter solstice, around {decSolstice}. The north end of Earth’s axis leans as far away from the Sun as it ever does. The yellow line from the Sun’s centre through Earth’s centre hits the Tropic of Capricorn.
graphicAlt: Side view of the Sun and Earth at the winter solstice. Parallel sunlight from the left. A solid yellow line from the Sun’s centre through Earth’s centre hits the Tropic of Capricorn. Dashed chords mark both tropics at plus and minus Earth’s tilt.

sections.heading: Why it sits at {tilt}° south
body: Whatever the Tropic of Cancer is for the north, the Tropic of Capricorn is for the south. Earth’s axis leans about {tilt}°. That lean never grows, so the Sun’s overhead point never crosses either tropic.

Around {decSolstice} the north end leans as far away from the Sun as it ever does, and the south end leans into the light. A ray from the centre of the Sun through the centre of Earth then hits this circle. That day is the winter solstice in the north — the shortest northern day, and summer in the south. The picture above is that day.

Between the two tropics, every place gets the Sun straight up on two days each year — once on the way north, once on the way back. Outside them, a vertical pole always casts some noon shadow, even on the longest day.

sections.heading: December, not a different Earth
body: Nothing about Earth changes between June and December except which end of the axis leans toward the light. When it is summer in Chile it is winter in Canada, on the same planet, at the same distance from the Sun. Distance is not the season.
The name Capricorn is the same kind of fossil as Cancer: the December-solstice Sun used to stand in that constellation. Precession moved the stars. The latitude stayed with the tilt.

question: What is the subsolar point?
shortAnswer: It is the one place on Earth where the Sun is straight overhead right now — where a flagpole casts no shadow. It is the yellow dot on the day/night map, and it is where the Sun-centre to Earth-centre line hits the surface.
ledeHtml: It is the one place on Earth where the Sun is straight overhead right now — where a flagpole casts no shadow. It is the yellow dot on the day/night map, and it is where the Sun-centre to Earth-centre line hits the surface.
title: What Is the Subsolar Point?
description: The subsolar point is where the Sun stands straight overhead. It races west once a day and drifts north and south once a year, never leaving the tropics.
graphicCaption: Sunlight arrives in parallel lines because the Sun is so far away. One of those lines is special: centre to centre. It meets Earth at a single point.
graphicAlt: Side view showing the yellow centre-to-centre line meeting Earth’s surface at the subsolar point.

sections.heading: A lap a day, a bounce a year
body: Earth turns. The overhead point therefore races west, once around the planet each day, at the speed of the ground under it — about 1,670 km/h at the equator.
It also drifts north and south with the seasons, because of the tilt. In June it reaches the Tropic of Cancer. In December it reaches the Tropic of Capricorn. It never leaves that band.

sections.heading: How this page finds it
body: The map does not look up a table of “where the Sun is.” It solves a low-precision solar series (the same one used for sunrise on this site): the Sun’s apparent ecliptic longitude, the obliquity, then declination and right ascension. Declination is the latitude of the subsolar point. Greenwich sidereal time turns right ascension into longitude.
That is why the yellow dot on the day/night map and the side-view hit are the same number. One series, two pictures.

seeItLive.label: Follow the yellow dot

question: What is the terminator?
shortAnswer: The terminator is the line between day and night — the circle on Earth where the Sun sits on the horizon. Sunrise is where you cross it going into the light; sunset is where you cross it going out.

teasers./: The curve of night on the map — it leans because Earth does.
teasers./earth/: Sunrise and sunset are this line crossing your town.

ledeHtml: The terminator is the line between day and night — the circle on Earth where the Sun sits on the horizon. Sunrise is where you cross it going into the light; sunset is where you cross it going out. On the day/night map it is the edge of the dark half.
title: What Is the Terminator?
description: The terminator is the day/night line: the circle where the Sun is on the horizon. It sweeps west as Earth turns, and it leans with the seasons.
graphicCaption: On the map the terminator is the edge of the dark half. It is a great circle on the globe; on this flat projection it becomes a wave that leans with the season.
graphicAlt: Equirectangular day and night map with the night side shaded and the terminator as the boundary of that shade.

sections.heading: A circle, drawn as a wave
body: On a globe the terminator is a circle: everywhere the Sun is exactly on the horizon. Half the planet is in front of it, half behind. Because sunlight arrives almost in parallel, that split is always half-and-half, whatever the date.

The map at the top of this site is flat, so the circle is stretched into a curve. Near an equinox the curve runs pole to pole. Near a solstice it leans, and one polar cap stays in daylight while the other stays dark.

sections.heading: How fast it moves
body: The line itself is not a thing racing over the ground. Earth is turning under a Sun that, for this purpose, sits still. At the equator that turn is about 1,670 km/h — 15 degrees of longitude per hour, which is why time zones are an hour wide.

This map solves the terminator per meridian: for each longitude, where is the Sun at altitude 0°? That is one equation in latitude. The shaded night is those latitudes closed toward the dark pole. Twilight is the same solve at −18°.

question: What is Earth’s axial tilt?
shortAnswer: Earth’s spin axis is not upright. It leans about 23.4° from the vertical to its orbit. That lean is why we have tropics, polar circles, and seasons — and it barely changes from one year to the next.

teasers./: The axis is not upright. That lean is why the tropics and the polar circles sit where they do.
teasers./earth/: The same number that sets the tropics is the lean in the orbit drawing above.

title: What Is Earth’s Axial Tilt?
description: Earth’s axial tilt is about 23.4°. The tropics sit at that latitude, the polar circles at 90° minus it, and the seasons are that lean facing toward or away from the Sun.
graphicCaption: The axis is drawn leaning by the Sun’s declination. That is not a sketch of the seasons. Seen from the orbital plane, that component of the tilt is what the seasons are.
graphicAlt: Earth seen from the side of its orbit, axis leaning, tropics as dashed chords at the tilt angle.

sections.heading: A lean that holds still
body: Hold a tilted spinning top and walk it around a lamp without twisting the tilt to follow the lamp. For half the walk the top’s north end points toward the light. For the other half it points away. That is the year.

The size of the lean is about 23.4° right now. This page does not type that number. It takes the largest declination in a year of the solar series — the same series that places the yellow dot on the day/night map.

sections.heading: It is slowly shrinking
body: The obliquity is 23.439° minus a tiny drift of 0.00000036° per day from the J2000 epoch. Over a human life you will not notice. Over millennia the tropics creep a few tenths of a degree. The four circles on the map would all move together.
What if the tilt were zero? Both tropics on the equator. Polar circles on the poles. The terminator always pole-to-pole. Every day the same length. No seasons. The lean is the whole of them.

question: What are the polar circles?
shortAnswer: The Arctic Circle and Antarctic Circle sit at 66.6° north and south — 90° minus Earth’s tilt. Inside them the Sun can stay up all day in summer, or stay down all day in winter.
title: What Are the Polar Circles?
description: The polar circles are at 90° minus Earth’s tilt, about 66.6° N and S. They are the other two circles written by the same 23.4° that draws the tropics.
graphicCaption: The Arctic Circle is the dashed line near the top of the map. The Antarctic Circle is cropped off this projection (the map cuts at 62° S) — the same tilt still puts it at 66.6° S on the globe.
graphicAlt: Day and night map with the Arctic Circle drawn as a dashed parallel near the top.

sections.heading: The same tilt, counted the other way
body: If the Sun’s overhead point never goes farther from the equator than the tilt, then at the poles the Sun never climbs farther from the horizon than the tilt either. Walk 23.4° down from the pole and you reach the first latitude where the Sun can just graze the horizon at midwinter and just refuse to set at midsummer. That walk is the polar circle.
So 90° − 23.4° = 66.6°. One subtraction. Two circles.

sections.heading: Midnight sun and polar night are not total darkness
body: Even when the Sun stays below the horizon, twilight can light the sky. Astronomical night — Sun 18° down — is a stricter line than “the Sun did not rise.” Near a solstice the twilight band on the map is wide at high latitudes, which is why a northern summer night is often not fully dark.

seeItLive.label: Find the Arctic Circle on the map

question: What is twilight?
shortAnswer: Twilight is the time when the Sun is below the horizon but still lighting the sky. This map draws it as a soft band: from the terminator down to where the Sun is 18° below — the edge of astronomical night.
title: What Is Twilight?
description: Twilight is sunlight scattered in the sky after sunset or before sunrise. Astronomical night begins when the Sun is 18° below the horizon.
graphicCaption: The map shades night (Sun below the horizon) and a second, paler band out to Sun altitude −18°. The ring between them is twilight. It is widest toward the poles.
graphicAlt: Day and night map with a hard night shade and a paler twilight band along the terminator.

sections.heading: Three common edges
body: Civil twilight: Sun 0° to 6° down — streetlights, a clear horizon. Nautical: 6° to 12° — the brighter stars, a usable sea horizon. Astronomical: 12° to 18° — the sky is not yet fully dark for faint objects. Past 18° down, night.
This map uses the far edge, −18°, so the band you see is the whole of twilight, not just the civil slice.

sections.heading: Why summer nights stay pale
body: At mid-latitudes the Sun dives steeply. Twilight is short. Near the polar circles the Sun skims the horizon, so it takes hours to fall 18°. In June, much of the north never reaches astronomical night at all. That is a geometry fact, not a weather one.

seeItLive.label: See the dusk band on the map

question: Why is this map flat?
shortAnswer: This map gives every degree of latitude and longitude the same length on the page, so meridians are straight and the terminator is honest. The cost is size: land near the poles is stretched. The picture says so, in numbers from the drawing.
ledeHtml: This day/night map gives every degree of latitude and longitude the same length on the page, so meridians are straight and the terminator is honest. The cost is size: land near the poles is stretched. The picture says so, in numbers from the drawing.
title: Why Is This Day/Night Map Flat?
description: The day/night map is equirectangular so meridians stay straight and the terminator can be solved per longitude. Continents near the poles are stretched on purpose.
graphicCaption: x = (longitude + 180) / 360 × width. y = (90 − latitude) / 180 × height. Every vertical line is a meridian. That is why this projection, and why Greenland looks huge.
graphicAlt: Flat world map with evenly spaced meridians and parallels, night shade solved per meridian.

sections.heading: Straight meridians are the point
body: A globe is the true shape. A page is not. This page’s job is to show where it is light, and that is a question asked in latitude and longitude. The projection that keeps those lines straight is equirectangular.
The poles are cropped (about 82° N to 62° S) because the top and bottom of a full 2:1 map are the most stretched bands, and no city this site cares about sits in them.

sections.heading: What that costs
body: On this drawing, a degree of latitude is the same length everywhere, but a degree of longitude shrinks by cos(latitude) on the real Earth and does not shrink here. At 60° the map is twice as wide as the ground. The page should say that whenever it talks about area.
The terminator solve does not care. It is done in latitude per meridian, then plotted. Stretching the picture does not move the answer.

seeItLive.label: Read the map with the stretch in mind

question: Why don’t planets fall into the Sun?
shortAnswer: They are falling. They are also moving sideways. By the time a planet has fallen, the Sun is no longer where it was falling toward. Falling and missing, without end, is an orbit. There is no outward force holding them up.

teasers./: They are falling. Missing is the rest of the sentence — sideways speed is what keeps the miss going.
teasers./space/: Slow a planet in the gravity card and the miss gets smaller. That is this question as a picture.

title: Why Don’t Planets Fall Into the Sun?
description: Planets fall toward the Sun and miss, forever. Sideways motion plus gravity is an orbit — not a balance with an outward push.
graphicCaption: A straight dashed path is what the planet would do with no gravity. A pull toward the Sun bends that path. The closed curve is the miss.
graphicAlt: Diagram of a planet’s sideways motion, a gravity arrow toward the Sun, and the resulting closed orbit.

sections.heading: Both halves of the question are fair
body: The Sun really is pulling every planet toward itself, constantly. Nothing is holding them up, so falling in is a fair expectation. And a planet really is moving fast enough that, with no gravity, it would sail off in a straight line. Flying away is a fair expectation too.
Both are happening. They do not cancel like two people pulling a rope. Gravity only changes the direction of the motion. The planet falls, and the ground it was falling toward has moved.

sections.heading: There is no outward force
body: Textbooks sometimes draw a centrifugal arrow. That arrow is a description in a spinning frame, not a second force out in space. In the inertial picture there is one force, inward, and a velocity, sideways. Newton’s first law does the rest.

seeItLive.label: Set a speed and watch the miss

question: How does an orbit work?
shortAnswer: A planet is always falling toward the Sun, and it is already moving sideways. Gravity only pulls inward — it never pushes the planet along. Those two together bend a straight line into a closed curve. That closed path is the orbit.

teasers./: Falling toward, already moving sideways. Change the sideways and the far side of the path is what moves.
teasers./space/: The Slow down / Speed up buttons on this card are the sentence above, runnable.

ledeHtml: A planet is always falling toward the Sun, and it is already moving sideways. Gravity only pulls inward — it never pushes the planet along. In the picture, the green arrow is the way it is already going. The gold arrow is the pull, always straight at the Sun. Press Slow down: the other side of the path falls toward the Sun, and the planet still comes back. That closed path is the orbit.
title: How Does an Orbit Work?
description: An orbit is falling toward the Sun and missing. Gravity pulls inward; sideways speed keeps the path from hitting. One speed at each distance makes a circle.
graphicCaption: The Sun stays where it is. You change the speed on the right. The other side of the path is what moves. Gold always points at the Sun; green is always sideways.
graphicAlt: The Sun at the centre of a circular orbit. A planet on the right has a green velocity arrow pointing along the path and a gold gravity arrow pointing at the Sun. Buttons play the orbit, slow it down, or speed it up.

sections.heading: Two arrows, not a balance
body: The gold arrow always points at the Sun. The green arrow is the way the planet is already going — and the dashed line is where it would go if gravity vanished for a moment. On a circle they stay at right angles, so gravity changes the planet’s direction without changing its speed. There is no outward force holding it up. Press Play and watch: gold stays aimed at the Sun while the planet goes around.
The Sun in the drawing is far larger than scale, on purpose. At an honest size its disc would be a fraction of a pixel, and you could not see what the planet is going around.

sections.heading: One speed at each distance
body: At Earth’s distance a circle needs about 29.8 km/s. Press Slow down: the far side of the orbit drops toward the Sun — the dashed circle is where it was — and the planet speeds up as it falls in. Press Speed up: the far side climbs away. Either way it comes back through the point where you changed it. That new path is an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus: not beside the path, and not at the empty middle of the oval.

sections.heading: What it takes to hit the Sun
body: Keep pressing Slow down. The ellipse gets longer and thinner. Only when almost all of that 29.8 km/s is gone does the near end reach the Sun. Nature almost never does that to a planet. Escape is the other end of the same slider: about 42 km/s at Earth’s distance, √2 times circular, and the path never closes.

A heavier planet is pulled harder, and is harder to turn, in exact proportion — so mass never appears on the controls. A grain of dust at Earth’s distance orbits at Earth’s speed. That is why the picture never asks you for a mass.

question: Why do we have seasons?
shortAnswer: Not because Earth gets closer to the Sun. When it is summer in the United States it is winter in Australia, on the same planet, at the same distance. Seasons happen because the axis is tilted 23.4° and keeps pointing the same way all year.

teasers./: Not because Earth gets closer to the Sun. Because it leans, and the lean faces a different way as it goes around.
teasers./earth/: Summer is the hemisphere leaned into the light — the orbit view above is that lean, running.
teasers./space/: Earth is not the only world that leans. The tilt is the season machine, and it is drawn here too.

title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
description: Seasons are the tilt, not the distance. Earth’s axis leans 23.4° and holds still, so each hemisphere takes a turn leaning into the sunlight.
graphicCaption: Earth goes around the Sun. The four marked positions are the start of each season. Spring sits on the orbit between the spring equinox and the summer solstice; summer, fall and winter follow the same way. Every Earth leans the same way, so sunlight falls on the north in June and the south in December. A yellow marker shows today’s place on the year.
graphicAlt: The Sun in the centre of Earth’s orbit. Four Earths mark the spring equinox, summer solstice, fall equinox and winter solstice, each leaning the same way so sunlight hits the north in June and the south in December. Season names sit on the orbit between them. A yellow marker shows today’s place on the year.

sections.heading: The test that kills the distance story
body: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January — northern winter. If distance ran the seasons, the whole planet would warm and cool together. It does not. One hemisphere’s summer is the other’s winter. The cause has to be a direction, not a distance.

sections.heading: Two effects, one lean
body: The lean does two things at once: it makes the day longer, and it raises the noon Sun. More hours, and each hour more concentrated on the ground. Neither is a change in how much light the Sun puts out.

seeItLive.label: Watch the day/night line lean with the year

question: Can the moon be up in the daytime?
shortAnswer: Yes. The moon is above the horizon about half of every day, and those hours drift through daylight as the month goes by. It is simply bright enough to beat the blue sky. On the day/night map the pale marker is where the moon stands overhead — watch it ride through the lit half.

teasers./: The Moon is up about twelve hours of every twenty-four, and those hours drift through the day.
teasers./earth/: Tonight's phase card above does not wait for dark.

ledeHtml: Yes. The moon is above the horizon about half of every day, and those hours drift through daylight as the month goes by. It is simply bright enough to beat the blue sky. On the day/night map the pale marker is where the moon stands overhead — watch it ride through the lit half.
title: Can the Moon Be Up in the Daytime?
description: The moon is up in daylight about as often as at night. It does not belong to the night; it just happens to be easier to notice then.
graphicCaption: The yellow marker is the sun, straight overhead. The pale marker is the moon. They are not opposites: near a new moon they sit close together, both in daylight.
graphicAlt: Day and night world map with the sun’s overhead point and the moon’s overhead point both marked.

sections.heading: The moon does not know about night
body: The moon goes around Earth once a month. For about twelve hours of every twenty-four it is above somebody’s horizon, and those twelve hours slide through the clock as the month goes on. Roughly half of all the time the moon is up is daytime.

You notice it more at night because the sky is dark. In daylight it is still there — a pale disc, bright enough to beat the blue. A crescent is hardest to spot; a fat gibbous moon in the afternoon is easy.

sections.heading: Where the map puts it
body: The pale marker on the day/night map is the sublunar point: the one place the moon stands straight overhead at the instant on the slider. It is the same idea as the yellow subsolar point, solved from the moon’s position rather than the sun’s.

Near new moon the two markers sit close together, both in the lit half — that is a daytime moon. Near full moon they sit on opposite sides of the world, so the moon is overhead at night. Press Play and watch the pale marker sweep; it will cross into daylight and back out again.
